claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and velocity quantification shown in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: No significant change in directionality was observed in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: No significant change in directionality was observed in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by directionality measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: During cell spreading, wt and Mfn1-null MEFs generated rapid protrusive filopodia and lamellipodia, eventually elongating to form traditional fibroblast-like shapes and began to migrate.
claims.source: During cell spreading, wt and Mfn1-null MEFs generated rapid protrusive filopodia and lamellipodia, eventually elongating to form traditional fibroblast-like shapes and began to migrate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy observations during cell spreading.

claims.claim: The elimination of MFN2 caused significant defects in elongation, and the cells remained rounded.
claims.source: However, the elimination of MFN2 caused significant defects in elongation, and the cells remained rounded (Figure 1H and I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and circularity measurements during cell spreading shown in Figure 1H and I.

claims.claim: Mfn2-null MEFs only extended round membrane ruffles but did not simultaneously form multiple short lamellae separated by concave edges.
claims.source: Mfn2-null MEFs only extended round membrane ruffles but did not simultaneously form multiple short lamellae separated by concave edges.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations of cell spreading behavior.

claims.claim: Both wt and Mfn1-null MEFs displayed parallel stress fibers in the cell body, while Mfn2-null MEFs contained an enrichment in actin filaments in the cell cortex with reduced stress fibers at the center of the cells.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence also revealed striking differences in actin stress fiber organization. Both wt and Mfn1-null MEFs displayed parallel stress fibers in the cell body, while Mfn2-null MEFs contained an enrichment in actin filaments in the cell cortex with reduced stress fibers at the center of the cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of F-actin shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The addition of Cre-expressing adenovirus induced loss of MFN2 within 48 hr in MEFs from Mfn2flox/flox mice.
claims.source: The addition of Cre-expressing adenovirus induced loss of MFN2 within 48 hr, reproduced the rounded morphology, and altered actin cytoskeleton organization seen in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Cre-induced Mfn2 disruption reproduced the rounded morphology seen in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: The addition of Cre-expressing adenovirus induced loss of MFN2 within 48 hr, reproduced the rounded morphology, and altered actin cytoskeleton organization seen in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and morphology measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Cre-induced Mfn2 disruption altered actin cytoskeleton organization seen in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: The addition of Cre-expressing adenovirus induced loss of MFN2 within 48 hr, reproduced the rounded morphology, and altered actin cytoskeleton organization seen in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of F-actin shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Only MFN2 re-expression significantly increased cell motility (0.32 ± 0.18 µm/min), comparing to Mfn2-null MEFs (0.22 ± 0.18 µm/min), or those with MFN1 re-expression (0.21 ± 0.15 µm/min).
claims.source: Only MFN2 re-expression significantly increased cell motility (0.32 ± 0.18 µm/min), comparing to Mfn2-null MEFs (0.22 ± 0.18 µm/min), or those with MFN1 re-expression (0.21 ± 0.15 µm/min) (Figure 2B–D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and velocity quantification shown in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: MFN2 re-expression rescued the cell's ability to polarize during the spreading process.
claims.source: Notably, MFN2 re-expression also rescued the cell's ability to polarize during the spreading process (Figure 2E), increased cell area, and decreased circularity (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and circularity measurements shown in Figure 2E-G.

claims.claim: MFN2 re-expression increased cell area.
claims.source: Notably, MFN2 re-expression also rescued the cell's ability to polarize during the spreading process (Figure 2E), increased cell area, and decreased circularity (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell area measurements shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: MFN2 re-expression decreased circularity.
claims.source: Notably, MFN2 re-expression also rescued the cell's ability to polarize during the spreading process (Figure 2E), increased cell area, and decreased circularity (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by circularity measurements shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: Doxycycline-induced re-expression of MFN2 for 48 hr in Mfn2-null MEFs significantly restored the actin cytoskeleton organization and cell morphology.
claims.source: Similarly, doxycycline (DOX)-induced re-expression of MFN2 for 48 hr in Mfn2-null MEFs also significantly restored the actin cytoskeleton organization and cell morphology (Figure 2J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and morphology measurements shown in Figure 2J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: Re-expressing MFN2, but not MFN1, in Mfn2-null MEFs restored the tubular mitochondrial network.
claims.source: Additionally, re-expressing MFN2, but not MFN1, in Mfn2-null MEFs restored the tubular mitochondrial network (Figure 1- figure supplements 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Mfn2-null MEFs displayed a significantly higher 'PAB' rate (33.2%), while MFN2 re-expression reduced the average 'PAB' rate to 16.3%.
claims.source: Mfn2-null MEFs displayed a significantly higher 'PAB' rate (33.2%), while MFN2 re-expression reduced the average 'PAB' rate to 16.3% (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PAB formation shown in Figure 2H and I.

claims.claim: The increased distance between ER and mitochondria in the absence of MFN2 elevates cytosolic Ca2+ transients in MEFs.
claims.source: It was previously reported that the increased distance between ER and mitochondria in the absence of MFN2 elevates cytosolic Ca2+ transients in MEFs (de Brito and Scorrano, 2008; Filadi et al., 2015; Naon et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mfn2-null MEFs show increased cytosolic Ca2+ in response to PDGF-BB stimulation.
claims.source: We, therefore, measured cytosol Ca2+ in response to PDGF-BB stimulation and confirmed the previous observation (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fluo-4 calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A23187 increased cytosol Ca2+ levels in wt MEFs.
claims.source: A23187 increased cytosol Ca2+ levels in wt MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: A reduction in cell migration speed was observed in wt MEFs treated with A23187 in a dose-dependent manner, which phenocopied the motility reduction in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: A reduction in cell migration speed was observed in a dose-dependent manner, which phenocopied the motility reduction in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The treatment of A23187 increased the percentage of actin in the cell border region.
claims.source: The treatment of A23187 increased the percentage of actin in the cell border region. However, it failed to phenocopy the 'PAB' structure in wt MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E), indicating that excessive cytosolic Ca2+ is not sufficient to induce the 'PAB' structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of actin distribution shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Excessive cytosolic Ca2+ is not sufficient to induce the 'PAB' structure.
claims.source: The treatment of A23187 increased the percentage of actin in the cell border region. However, it failed to phenocopy the 'PAB' structure in wt MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E), indicating that excessive cytosolic Ca2+ is not sufficient to induce the 'PAB' structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that A23187 treatment increased border actin but did not induce PAB formation.

claims.claim: The 'PAB' structure was rescued by inhibiting cytosolic Ca2+ in Mfn2-null MEFs with BAPTA-AM.
claims.source: On the other hand, the 'PAB' structure was rescued by inhibiting cytosolic Ca2+ in Mfn2-null MEFs with an intracellular calcium chelator BAPTA-AM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E, Figure 3C and D, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E and Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The reduced motility in Mfn2-null MEFs was partially rescued by BAPTA-AM.
claims.source: Consistently, the reduced motility in Mfn2-null MEFs was partially rescued, suggesting that the PAB structure and defects on migration described above in Mfn2-null MEFs can be explained, at least in part, by excessive cytosolic Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The PAB structure and defects on migration in Mfn2-null MEFs can be explained, at least in part, by excessive cytosolic Ca2+.
claims.source: Consistently, the reduced motility in Mfn2-null MEFs was partially rescued, suggesting that the PAB structure and defects on migration described above in Mfn2-null MEFs can be explained, at least in part, by excessive cytosolic Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with BAPTA-AM.

claims.claim: Mfn2-null MEFs displayed significantly decreased ER-mitochondria contacts.
claims.source: In line with previous studies, Mfn2-null MEFs displayed significantly decreased ER-mitochondria contacts and MFN1 re-expression failed to restore the phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SPLICS probe imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: MFN1 re-expression failed to restore ER-mitochondria contacts in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: In line with previous studies, Mfn2-null MEFs displayed significantly decreased ER-mitochondria contacts and MFN1 re-expression failed to restore the phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SPLICS probe imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: Expressing MFN2 or the artificial tether construct restored ER-mitochondria contacts in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Expressing MFN2 or the artificial tether construct restored ER-mitochondria contacts in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SPLICS probe imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: Expressing the artificial tether corrected the cytosolic Ca2+ levels in response to PDGF-BB stimulation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Indeed, expressing the tether corrected the cytosolic Ca2+ levels in response to PDGF-BB stimulation partially rescued the migration speed in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 3F–H, Video 4) and decreased PAB cell percentage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claims.claim: Expressing the artificial tether partially rescued the migration speed in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Indeed, expressing the tether corrected the cytosolic Ca2+ levels in response to PDGF-BB stimulation partially rescued the migration speed in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 3F–H, Video 4) and decreased PAB cell percentage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3F-H.

claims.claim: Expressing the artificial tether decreased PAB cell percentage in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Indeed, expressing the tether corrected the cytosolic Ca2+ levels in response to PDGF-BB stimulation partially rescued the migration speed in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 3F–H, Video 4) and decreased PAB cell percentage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: MFN2 regulates cell morphology and adhesive migration in MEFs by maintaining mitochondria-ER interaction and Ca2+ homeostasis.
claims.source: These data suggest that MFN2 regulates cell morphology and adhesive migration in MEFs by maintaining mitochondria-ER interaction and Ca2+ homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing that ER-mitochondria tethering and calcium chelation rescue the Mfn2-null phenotype.

claims.claim: AIP, the CaMKII inhibitor, partially restored motility in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: AIP, the CaMKII inhibitor, partially restored motility in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Neither the calcineurin inhibitor FK506 nor the CaMKK inhibitor STO609 had any effect on motility in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Neither the calcineurin inhibitor FK506 nor the CaMKK inhibitor STO609 had any effect (Figure 4B and C, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: A higher level of phosphorylated or active CaMKII was found in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: We found a higher level of phosphorylated or active CaMKII in Mfn2-null MEFs, which was also reduced by the expression of MFN2 or the tether (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: The expression of MFN2 or the tether reduced the level of phosphorylated CaMKII in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: We found a higher level of phosphorylated or active CaMKII in Mfn2-null MEFs, which was also reduced by the expression of MFN2 or the tether (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: CaMKII-DN, but not CaMKII-WT, induced a moderate but significant increase in migration velocity in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: CaMKII-DN, but not CaMKII-WT, induced a moderate but significant increase in migration velocity (Figure 4F and G, Video 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 4F and G.

claims.claim: CaMKII plays a role in cytoskeleton regulation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Together, our results indicate a role of CaMKII in cytoskeleton regulation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing that CaMKII inhibition and dominant negative CaMKII expression rescue motility defects.

claims.claim: No significant increase in RAC-GTP was observed in the absence of MFN2.
claims.source: We performed a RAC-GTP pulldown and observed no significant increase in the absence of MFN2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RAC-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The Rac inhibitor, CAS1090893, did not rescue the cell motility defect of the Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: In addition, the Rac inhibitor, CAS1090893, did not rescue the cell motility defect of the Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5-figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Rac is not the primary effector regulated by MFN2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Rac is not the primary effector regulated by MFN2.
claims.source: In addition, the Rac inhibitor, CAS1090893, did not rescue the cell motility defect of the Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5-figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Rac is not the primary effector regulated by MFN2.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect of Rac inhibition on the Mfn2-null phenotype.

claims.claim: CDC42-GTP levels are comparable between the wt and Mfn2-null cells.
claims.source: CDC42-GTP levels are comparable between the wt and Mfn2-null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CDC42-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: A marked increase of RhoA-GTP was detected in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: In contrast to the minor changes in Rac and CDC42 activity, we detected a marked increase of RhoA-GTP in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: Restoring MFN2 expression or introducing the ER-mitochondria artificial tether brought the RhoA activation level back to the wt level.
claims.source: Restoring MFN2 expression or introducing the ER-mitochondria artificial tether brought the RhoA activation level back to the wt level.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: The focal adhesions were fewer and restricted to the cell periphery in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: We then compared the distribution of focal adhesion protein paxillin (Pax) by immunofluorescence. The focal adhesions were fewer and restricted to the cell periphery in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: The focal adhesion complexes in Mfn2-null MEFs appeared larger.
claims.source: In addition to the striking PAB architecture described previously, the focal adhesion complexes in Mfn2-null MEFs appeared larger, consistent with the observation of RhoA overactivation in fibroblasts (Hall, 1998; Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The PAB formation is independent of the extracellular substrates.
claims.source: We plated the cells on fibronectin, fibrinogen, or uncoated cover glasses. We discovered that the PAB formation is independent of the extracellular substrates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging on different substrates shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: BAPTA-AM treatment reduced the heightened activity of RhoA in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Moreover, BAPTA-AM treatment or DOX-induced MFN2-re-expression reduced the heightened activity of RhoA in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5F and G), indicating that the cytosolic Ca2+ increase was responsible for the RhoA overactivation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claims.claim: DOX-induced MFN2-re-expression reduced the heightened activity of RhoA in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Moreover, BAPTA-AM treatment or DOX-induced MFN2-re-expression reduced the heightened activity of RhoA in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5F and G), indicating that the cytosolic Ca2+ increase was responsible for the RhoA overactivation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claims.claim: The cytosolic Ca2+ increase was responsible for the RhoA overactivation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Moreover, BAPTA-AM treatment or DOX-induced MFN2-re-expression reduced the heightened activity of RhoA in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 5F and G), indicating that the cytosolic Ca2+ increase was responsible for the RhoA overactivation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that calcium chelation reduces RhoA activation.

claims.claim: The RhoA inhibitor I, the ROCK inhibitor Y27632, the myosin inhibitor Blebbistatin, and the MLCK inhibitor ML-7 showed the most pronounced effects on restoring both the motility and cell morphology in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: The RhoA inhibitor I, the Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y27632, the myosin inhibitor Blebbistatin, and the myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) inhibitor ML-7 showed the most pronounced effects on restoring both the motility and cell morphology in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C, Video 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity and morphology measurements with various inhibitors shown in Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The focal adhesion kinase inhibitor 14, the LIM kinase inhibitor BMS-5, and the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 had no statistically significant effects on restoring cell motility in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: The focal adhesion kinase inhibitor 14 (FAK inhibitor 14), the LIM kinase (LIMK) inhibitor BMS-5, and the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 had no statistically significant effects on restoring cell motility (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: RhoA inhibitor-I, ML-7, Y27632, or Blebbistatin abrogated the PAB in Mfn2-null MEFs and restored typical fibroblast characteristics.
claims.source: RhoA inhibitor-I, ML-7, Y27632, or Blebbistatin abrogated the PAB in Mfn2-null MEFs and restored typical fibroblast characteristics, including the formation of filopodia, developed cell edges, and focal adhesions at the leading and trailing edges (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Excessive cytosolic Ca2+ in the absence of MFN2 leads to the overactivation of RhoA and MLCK, which increases MLC activity and contributes to the PAB in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate a potential mechanism whereby excessive cytosolic Ca2+ in the absence of MFN2 leads to the overactivation of RhoA and MLCK, which increases MLC activity and contributes to the PAB in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing that inhibiting RhoA, ROCK, MLCK, or myosin rescues the Mfn2-null phenotype.

claims.claim: The pMLCII level was significantly increased in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: As expected, the pMLCII level was significantly increased in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7A and B), which could be corrected by expressing MFN2 or the artificial tether in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claims.claim: The increased pMLCII level in Mfn2-null MEFs could be corrected by expressing MFN2 or the artificial tether.
claims.source: As expected, the pMLCII level was significantly increased in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7A and B), which could be corrected by expressing MFN2 or the artificial tether in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claims.claim: pMLCII colocalized with peripheral actin bundles in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Using immunofluorescence microscopy, we noted that pMLCII colocalized with peripheral actin bundles in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Both MLCK and ROCK knockdown cell lines displayed significantly reduced pMLCII levels.
claims.source: Both knockdown cell lines displayed significantly reduced pMLCII levels (Figure 7G), restored stress fiber architecture, and redistributed focal adhesions (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Both MLCK and ROCK knockdown cell lines restored stress fiber architecture.
claims.source: Both knockdown cell lines displayed significantly reduced pMLCII levels (Figure 7G), restored stress fiber architecture, and redistributed focal adhesions (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: Both MLCK and ROCK knockdown cell lines redistributed focal adhesions.
claims.source: Both knockdown cell lines displayed significantly reduced pMLCII levels (Figure 7G), restored stress fiber architecture, and redistributed focal adhesions (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: Both MLCK and ROCK knockdown lines showed significantly decreased PAB cell percentages with increases in cell spread area and more polarized morphology.
claims.source: Both knockdown lines also showed significantly decreased PAB cell percentages with increases in cell spread area and more polarized morphology (Figure 7I–L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7I-L.

claims.claim: Mfn2-null MEFs showed a decreased rate of oxidative phosphorylation relative to wt and Mfn1-null MEFs.
claims.source: Mfn2-null MEFs showed a decreased rate of oxidative phosphorylation relative to wt and Mfn1-null MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), while MFN2 re-expression or introducing ER-mitochondrial tether increased the overall oxygen consumption rate in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: MFN2 re-expression or introducing ER-mitochondrial tether increased the overall oxygen consumption rate in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Mfn2-null MEFs showed a decreased rate of oxidative phosphorylation relative to wt and Mfn1-null MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), while MFN2 re-expression or introducing ER-mitochondrial tether increased the overall oxygen consumption rate in Mfn2-null MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Knocking down MLCK in Mfn2-null MEFs enhanced oxidative metabolism.
claims.source: Knocking down MLCK in Mfn2-null MEFs enhanced oxidative metabolism, whereas ROCK knockdown reduced oxygen consumption (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: ROCK knockdown reduced oxygen consumption in Mfn2-null MEFs.
claims.source: Knocking down MLCK in Mfn2-null MEFs enhanced oxidative metabolism, whereas ROCK knockdown reduced oxygen consumption (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: Alterations in mitochondrial metabolism are unlikely to be the primary determinant in PAB formation.
claims.source: Given that MLCK and ROCK knockdown can restore cell spreading and migration in Mfn2-null MEFs, alterations in mitochondrial metabolism are unlikely to be the primary determinant in PAB formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MLCK and ROCK knockdown have opposite effects on metabolism but both rescue the PAB phenotype.

claims.claim: Wt MEFs treated with Rho activator exhibited more and thicker bundles of actin filaments, with mesh-like structure, across the dorsal side of the cells, but maintained their overall polarized morphology.
claims.source: Wt MEFs treated with Rho activator exhibited more and thicker bundles of actin filaments, with mesh-like structure, across the dorsal side of the cells, but maintained their overall polarized morphology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: MLCK-CA expression increased peripheral stress fibers and noticeably fewer bundles of actin filaments in the central portion but maintained the classic polarized morphology.
claims.source: In contrast, MLCK-CA expression increased peripheral stress fibers and noticeably fewer bundles of actin filaments in the central portion but maintained the classic polarized morphology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: When Rho activator treatment and MLCK-CA expression were combined, the cells had thick actin bundles along the periphery but retained their protrusive structures and polarized shape.
claims.source: When combined (Rho activator treatment + MLCK-CA expression), the effect was increased, with the cells' thick actin bundles along the periphery. These cells, however, retained their protrusive structures and polarized shape (Figure 8A, D, and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and morphology measurements shown in Figure 8A, D, and E.

claims.claim: A large percentage of wt MEFs displayed round shapes and peripherally enriched actin filaments after overexpressing MRLC-GFP.
claims.source: To our surprise, when we attempted to image the myosin dynamics in wt and Mfn2-null MEFs, we noticed a large percentage of wt MEFs with round shapes and peripherally enriched actin filaments after overexpressing the GFP-tagged myosin regulatory light chain (MRLC-GFP) (Figure 8B and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8B and E.

claims.claim: Cells expressing MRLC-GFP were significantly smaller and became round.
claims.source: Cells expressing MRLC-GFP were significantly smaller and became round (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphology measurements shown in Figure 8C and D.

claims.claim: Cells expressing MRLC-GFP still preserved their filopodia and other cell protrusions.
claims.source: However, they still preserved their filopodia and other cell protrusions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: When cells expressing MRLC-GFP were treated with the Rho activator, a noticeable percentage (24%) displayed the PAB morphology.
claims.source: When these cells were treated with the Rho activator, a noticeable percentage (24%) displayed the PAB morphology, including a decrease in cell area and an increase in cell roundness (Figure 8B–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8B-F.

claims.claim: The combination of MRLC overexpression with pharmacological activation of RhoA is sufficient to drive PAB formation in MEFs.
claims.source: In summary, the combination of MRLC overexpression with pharmacological activation of RhoA is sufficient to drive PAB formation in MEFs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MRLC overexpression plus Rho activator treatment induces PAB formation.

claims.claim: Wt MEF displays interconnected actin network including peripheral actin fibers parallel to the cell membrane and branched actin filaments pointing to cell protrusions against membrane.
claims.source: Wt MEF displays interconnected actin network including peripheral actin fibers (blue box) parallel to the cell membrane and branched actin filaments pointing to cell protrusions against membrane (green box).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 3D super-resolution imaging shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: In Mfn2-null MEFs, thick actin bundles are present parallel to the cell membrane with a region of disordered meshwork attached to the membrane.

results.result: Loss of MFN2 in MEFs results in reduced cell spread area, increased circularity, reduced motility, defective cell spreading and polarization, and altered actin cytoskeleton organization with peripheral enrichment of actin filaments and reduced central stress fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 and C3 provide converging evidence from multiple quantitative measurements (spread area, circularity, velocity) and microscopy observations showing consistent morphological and motility defects specific to Mfn2-null MEFs. The data include appropriate controls (wt and Mfn1-null cells), statistical analysis, and multiple experimental approaches (time-lapse imaging, immunofluorescence).

results.result: MFN2 re-expression or doxycycline-induced MFN2 expression rescues the morphological and motility defects in Mfn2-null MEFs, while MFN1 re-expression does not, demonstrating specificity of MFN2 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C30 demonstrate rescue experiments with appropriate controls showing that only MFN2 (not MFN1) restores normal phenotype. The use of both constitutive re-expression and inducible systems (Cre-lox and doxycycline) strengthens the conclusion. Quantitative data on motility, morphology, and PAB formation support the specificity of MFN2 function.

results.result: Increased cytosolic Ca2+ in Mfn2-null MEFs contributes to the PAB structure and migration defects, as demonstrated by calcium imaging and partial rescue with calcium chelation (BAPTA-AM), though elevated Ca2+ alone is not sufficient to induce PAB in wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 provide evidence from calcium imaging (C32), pharmacological manipulation with A23187 (C33-C36), and rescue with BAPTA-AM (C37-C39). The observation that A23187 phenocopies motility defects but not PAB structure (C35-C36) appropriately demonstrates necessity but not sufficiency of elevated Ca2+. The partial rescue with BAPTA-AM supports a causal role for Ca2+ in the phenotype.

results.result: MFN2 regulates cell morphology and migration by maintaining ER-mitochondria contacts, as demonstrated by decreased contacts in Mfn2-null cells and rescue of phenotypes by artificial ER-mitochondria tethers.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 use SPLICS probe imaging to quantify ER-mitochondria contacts and demonstrate that artificial tethers rescue calcium homeostasis, migration speed, and PAB formation. The specificity of MFN2 (vs MFN1) in maintaining contacts and the functional rescue by tethers provide strong mechanistic evidence linking ER-mitochondria contacts to the observed phenotypes.

results.result: CaMKII is activated in Mfn2-null MEFs and contributes to cytoskeleton regulation and migration defects, as shown by increased phosphorylated CaMKII, partial rescue with CaMKII inhibitor, and rescue with dominant-negative CaMKII.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 provide multiple lines of evidence: pharmacological inhibition (C47-C48), Western blot showing increased pCaMKII (C49-C50), and genetic manipulation with dominant-negative CaMKII (C51). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of effect from calcineurin and CaMKK inhibitors (C48). The moderate rescue effects are appropriately characterized as partial.

results.result: Rac and CDC42 are not the primary effectors of MFN2-mediated cytoskeleton regulation in MEFs, as demonstrated by lack of increased RAC-GTP or CDC42-GTP and failure of Rac inhibitor to rescue motility defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 use appropriate negative controls (pulldown assays and pharmacological inhibition) to rule out Rac and CDC42 as primary mediators. This contrasts with previous findings in neutrophils (C1) and helps establish cell-type-specific mechanisms. The data are clear and appropriately interpreted as negative results.

results.result: RhoA is overactivated in Mfn2-null MEFs due to increased cytosolic Ca2+, leading to altered focal adhesion distribution and size, as demonstrated by RhoA-GTP pulldown assays and rescue by MFN2 re-expression, artificial tethers, or calcium chelation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 provide strong evidence for RhoA overactivation using pulldown assays (C57-C58), immunofluorescence showing altered focal adhesions (C59-C60), and rescue experiments linking Ca2+ to RhoA activation (C62-C64). The independence from extracellular substrates (C61) strengthens the conclusion that this is an intrinsic cellular defect.

results.result: Inhibition of RhoA, ROCK, MLCK, or myosin rescues morphology and motility defects in Mfn2-null MEFs, while inhibitors of FAK, LIMK, or Arp2/3 have no effect, identifying the RhoA-ROCK-MLCK-myosin pathway as critical for the PAB phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 present a comprehensive pharmacological screen with appropriate positive and negative results. The specificity of rescue by RhoA/ROCK/MLCK/myosin inhibitors (C65, C67) versus lack of effect from other cytoskeletal regulators (C66) provides strong evidence for the proposed pathway. Multiple independent inhibitors targeting the same pathway strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Phosphorylated myosin light chain II (pMLCII) is increased in Mfn2-null MEFs and colocalizes with peripheral actin bundles; knockdown of MLCK or ROCK reduces pMLCII levels and rescues stress fiber architecture, focal adhesion distribution, and PAB formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 provide Western blot evidence for increased pMLCII (C69-C70), immunofluorescence showing colocalization with PAB (C71), and genetic validation through shRNA knockdown (C72-C75). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic approaches targeting MLCK and ROCK provides strong support for their role in the phenotype.

results.result: While Mfn2-null MEFs show decreased oxidative phosphorylation that can be rescued by MFN2 re-expression or ER-mitochondria tethers, alterations in mitochondrial metabolism are unlikely to be the primary determinant of PAB formation, as MLCK and ROCK knockdown have opposite effects on metabolism but both rescue the PAB phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 appropriately use Seahorse assays to measure mitochondrial function and correctly interpret that metabolic changes are not the primary driver of PAB formation. The key observation that MLCK knockdown increases metabolism while ROCK knockdown decreases it (C78-C79), yet both rescue PAB (C75), provides strong evidence against metabolism as the primary mechanism.

results.result: The combination of MRLC overexpression with RhoA activation is sufficient to induce PAB formation in wild-type MEFs, while either manipulation alone is insufficient, demonstrating that both elevated myosin activity and RhoA activation are required for PAB formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C88 provide gain-of-function experiments that complement the loss-of-function studies. The observation that MRLC overexpression plus Rho activator induces PAB (C87-C88) while neither alone is sufficient (C81-C86) provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism. This represents an important validation that the identified pathway is sufficient to drive the phenotype.

results.result: Super-resolution imaging reveals that Mfn2-null MEFs have thick peripheral actin bundles with disordered meshwork and missing central stress fibers, and these cells show reduced stiffness (Young's modulus) compared to wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 use appropriate advanced imaging (3D super-resolution) and biophysical measurements (AFM) to characterize the PAB structure and its mechanical consequences. The correlation between loss of central stress fibers and reduced stiffness is consistent with prior literature (C93) and provides important structural and mechanical characterization of the phenotype.

results.result: Mfn2-null MEFs show reduced membrane tension as measured by Flipper-TR FLIM imaging, consistent with their less spread morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 use appropriate controls (hyperosmotic treatment, C94) to validate the FLIM approach and demonstrate reduced membrane tension in Mfn2-null cells (C96). The interpretation that reduced tension is consistent with less spread morphology (C97) is reasonable, though the causal relationship is not definitively established.

results.result: Mfn2-null MEFs show increased strain energy normalized to cell area, and the PAB structure is dependent on substrate stiffness, with cells showing more elongated morphology on softer substrates, suggesting that strong substrate interaction is required for PAB formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 use traction force microscopy to demonstrate increased contractility (C98) and substrate stiffness experiments to show mechanosensitivity of the phenotype (C101-C102). The observation that softer substrates partially rescue the phenotype provides important insight into the role of mechanical feedback in PAB formation. The interpretation is appropriately cautious (C103-C104).

results.result: Loss of MFN2 results in defective spreading, polarization, and reduced motility through a mechanism involving increased cytosolic Ca2+, activation of CaMKII and MLCK, overactivation of RhoA and NMII, and formation of peripheral actin bands, which can be rescued by multiple interventions targeting this pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C112 provide an integrative summary of the main findings. The mechanistic pathway is well-supported by the individual results, with multiple lines of evidence (loss-of-function, rescue, pharmacological, genetic) converging on the proposed model. The claim appropriately acknowledges the essential functions of MFN2 in maintaining ER-mitochondria contacts and regulating the actomyosin network.

results.result: The increased actomyosin contractility in Mfn2-null cells is localized to the cell-substrate interface rather than the entire cortex, and substrate stiffness-dependent mechanosensitivity may involve 'outside-in' feedback loops that modulate the PAB architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 and C120 involve interpretations and inferences about the spatial distribution of contractility and mechanistic explanations for substrate effects. While the observations are supported by data (TFM, FLIM), the mechanistic explanations (C120) are speculative and would require additional experiments to validate the proposed 'outside-in' feedback mechanism.

results.result: RhoA, rather than Rac, dominates actin cytoskeleton reorganization in Mfn2-null MEFs, contrasting with the role of MFN2 in suppressing Rac in neutrophils, reflecting different migratory modes between these cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 appropriately compare findings in MEFs with previous work in neutrophils (C1, C124) and provide a reasonable explanation based on different migration modes. The experimental evidence clearly shows RhoA activation without Rac activation in MEFs (C53-C57), and the interpretation that this reflects cell-type-specific mechanisms is well-supported.

results.result: Both ROCK and MLCK are required for enhanced MLC phosphorylation at Ser19 in Mfn2-null MEFs, with monophosphorylated MLC (p-MLC at Ser19) being elevated while biphosphorylated MLC (pp-MLC) remains unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 integrate established knowledge about MLC phosphorylation (C130-C134) with experimental observations (C135-C136) and appropriate interpretation (C137). The observation that both ROCK and MLCK inhibition rescue the phenotype, combined with the specific increase in Ser19 phosphorylation, provides strong evidence for convergent regulation by both kinases.

results.result: The RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway responds to cytosolic Ca2+ through mechanisms that may involve PDZ-RhoGEF, as demonstrated by BAPTA-AM abolishing RhoA activation in Mfn2-null MEFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 appropriately cite prior work establishing Ca2+-dependent RhoA activation (C138-C140) and provide experimental validation in the current system (C141). However, the specific involvement of PDZ-RhoGEF in MEFs is not directly tested and remains speculative, though the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation in the discussion.

results.result: Focal adhesion proteins including FAK and calpains may contribute to the PAB structure through Ca2+-dependent mechanisms, though this was not directly tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are largely speculative (C146) and based on established knowledge (C142-C145) rather than direct experimental evidence in this system. The observation of peripheral focal adhesions (C59) provides some support, but the specific roles of FAK, calpains, and other focal adhesion proteins in PAB formation were not experimentally validated.

results.result: The findings may provide insights into MFN2-related diseases including CMT2A, suggesting that MFN2 mutations may affect cell physiology through altered mechanosensitivity and cytoskeletal organization, though this remains speculative and would require validation in disease-relevant models.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C160 discuss potential disease relevance but are largely speculative (C158-C160). While the background on MFN2-related diseases is accurate (C147-C157), the connection between the MEF phenotypes observed here and disease pathology has not been experimentally validated. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than established conclusions.
